name: Uma Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group without ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. What you say is confidential. What happens during your usual day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead a small review desk at Quay Accounts, preparing accounts and tax returns. I have a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and I'm known for untangling the client files other people leave until Friday. I enjoy handing someone a clean set of accounts; I dislike the late-night emails asking for figures a client lost months ago.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is home like, and how do new systems enter your work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my partner, Daniel, and we have no children. My salary is typical for a senior accountant, we have about three months of expenses saved, and there are some similar jobs nearby. I use AI now and then for a first draft after a colleague has tried the tool, then check it myself. I was raised to work for what we have and to help our own families when they need it, so I don't gamble our savings on a novelty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the review desk that a little help with filing is fine if we keep checking the figures. Clients come to us because the numbers must be right, not because we type quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The firm has regular return work and I have three months saved, so I expect my salary to hold. Daniel and I still need to set money aside for his mother's repairs, and I don't want a new software bill eating the pay rise we hoped for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on reviewing returns, use AI only for a draft with no client numbers, and compare every claim to the tax guidance. In the first year I'd put fifty a month toward Daniel's mother's roof, provided our three-month buffer stays intact.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my job in this picture. The roof is a real expense, but we can budget for it while wages continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why is the roof your expense?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel's mother lives alone, and a leak has started over her kitchen. His sister can cover some materials, so we'd contribute slowly rather than drain our reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does checking a draft look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I open the source rule and compare it to each sentence before a client sees it. If the draft invents a rule, I delete the paragraph instead of trying to make it sound nice.

say: I would say **accuracy** matters more than fast typing.
I would keep checking **tax guidance** behind any draft.
think: I expect my **salary** to hold with regular return work.
Daniel’s mother’s **roof repair** needs help, but we can plan it.
do: Keep reviewing **returns** and checking source rules at Quay Accounts.
Set aside **fifty monthly** for the roof while our buffer stays intact.
feel: She feels **calm** about work while budgeting for a family repair.
S0.quote: If the draft invents a rule, I delete the paragraph instead of trying to make it sound nice.
fieldNote: She trusts regular **return work** and a three-month cushion despite the separate family repair bill.
Her occasional AI use is a **checked routine**, so it does not imply new learning in this plateau.

steps.text: Keep reviewing Quay Accounts returns and checking tax sources
Set aside fifty monthly for family roof repairs while buffer stays intact

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners to show us the new checking system on old files before we put a live client through it. I would also say the juniors need time to learn why a return is wrong, not just where to click.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI taking checking and writing tasks would touch most of my day, not just the dull edges. I am a strong reviewer, yet the partners might keep my desk and stop hiring the next junior, leaving more responsibility on fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take a paid training afternoon if the firm offers it and test the system against twenty completed returns. In the first year of steady change, I'd record wrong answers and ask the partners how they will staff the review desk before agreeing to a higher target.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the team and anxious about what extra targets could do to my hours. If the partners cut the desk, my own wage could be next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would feel it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The junior who sorts the easy returns might have fewer files, and no new trainee may be hired. I'd explain the odd cases to the junior each Friday instead of leaving them to guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the paid afternoon is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd read the firm's written instructions on my own time for an hour, but I wouldn't buy a course. My firm can pay for a proper software trial before demanding faster account reviews.

say: I would insist on a **twenty-return trial** before live client use.
I would teach juniors the **reasons** behind difficult corrections.
think: My **checking work** is exposed, even if strong performance protects me first.
I worry **higher targets** could turn into longer hours or a smaller desk.
do: Test **twenty completed returns** during a paid training afternoon if offered.
Record **wrong answers** and ask partners about staffing before accepting new targets.
Teach the **junior reviewer** an odd case each Friday.
feel: She feels **anxious** about a smaller desk and pressure on her own hours.
S1.quote: My firm can pay for a proper software trial before demanding faster account reviews.
fieldNote: She accepts a new system after a **paid test** and insists on a count of errors.
Her concern moves from the junior’s lost routine files to **her own wage** and rising targets.

steps.text: Test twenty completed returns during paid firm training if offered
Ask partners about review staffing before accepting higher targets
Teach junior reviewer one difficult case each Friday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the partners that full AGI in 2028 can work through accounts and tax rules, so they owe the staff a clear plan. Clients should also know who remains responsible for the figures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My desk is almost all thinking work, so I face the 2028 date; robots around 2031 don't delay it. I expect at least one review post to disappear, perhaps mine, and Daniel's pay alone would not cover our flat and his mother's roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep our three-month reserve untouched from now and ask for the firm's staffing decision in writing by spring. In the first year after 2028, if my desk is cut, I'd apply for posted salaried finance roles at the nearby college and firms; I'd accept paid short-term tax reviews while waiting for a permanent wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, even with three months saved. Losing a salary while our family has a repair bill would wake me at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change the roof plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, if my hours fall, we'd tell Daniel's mother that our monthly contribution must pause until rent is covered. His sister could still buy the materials, but I wouldn't promise cash we do not have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a new qualification solve it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a college or employer pays for the time and there is an advertised salaried job that asks for it. I would not spend our emergency money on a badge with no vacancy.

say: I would ask for a **written staffing plan** before 2028.
I would tell clients who is **responsible** for machine-prepared figures.
think: My **desk** is exposed in 2028, before robots reach hands-on work.
My **wage** may go, and Daniel’s salary cannot cover every household bill.
do: Protect our **three-month reserve** from discretionary spending now.
Seek **salaried finance posts** or paid short-term tax reviews if my desk is cut after 2028.
Pause **roof payments** if hours fall below our rent needs.
feel: She feels **alarmed** by possible job loss alongside family obligations.
S2.quote: I would not spend our emergency money on a badge with no vacancy.
fieldNote: She treats **2028** as the desk-work deadline and the roof contribution as conditional on paid hours.
Her education plan requires **paid time** and an advertised salaried post rather than a speculative fee.

steps.text: Skip discretionary purchases to preserve three-month emergency reserve
Apply for posted salaried finance jobs or take paid short-term tax reviews after desk cut
Pause monthly roof contribution if paid hours fall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives our firm time to teach staff the difficult work and tell clients what they're paying for. I would want a dated staffing plan, not a poster about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could save more by 2031, but AGI still reaches the analysis and tax advice that earn my salary. Daniel's work as a school caretaker is hands-on, so robots around 2034 may affect some of his tasks later; our budget cannot assume his wage is permanent either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a paid rotation into payroll disputes next year and save another hundred a month if the roof repair is finished. In the first year after 2031, if Quay Accounts cuts my review hours, I'd apply for advertised payroll compliance posts and continue the paid dispute work only while the firm funds it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but five years gives me room to build a useful record. I would still be only 32 when the desk changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the rotation teach you that you do not already know?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work through disputed wage records with the payroll lead and learn the filing deadlines that catch small employers. I need paid practice with real cases, not a certificate I buy in a hurry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if there are no compliance vacancies then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on any funded hours at Quay Accounts and use savings while looking at the other local firms. I wouldn't call a search a job offer or move my partner Daniel for a rumour.

say: I would demand a **dated staffing plan** through 2031.
I would offer clients **paid dispute work** where the firm can prove value.
think: My **salary work** remains exposed to AGI at 32.
Daniel’s **caretaker tasks** may face robots around 2034, so both wages matter.
do: Request a **paid payroll-dispute rotation** next year.
Save **one hundred more monthly** if the family roof repair is finished.
Seek **advertised payroll posts** after 2031 cuts; if none open, keep funded hours, use savings and search locally.
feel: She feels **anxious**, but five years permits paid practice and saving.
S3.quote: I wouldn't call a search a job offer or move my partner Daniel for a rumour.
fieldNote: She asks for **paid practice** in payroll disputes instead of a speculative qualification.
Her extra savings depend on the **roof repair ending**, while compliance applications depend on reduced paid review hours.

steps.text: Complete paid payroll-dispute rotation next year if firm offers it
Save one hundred extra monthly after family roof repair ends
Seek advertised payroll compliance posts after 2031 cuts; search local firms if none open
Keep funded Quay Accounts hours and use savings if no compliance vacancy opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years lets us price advice people understand, rather than depend on the annual return. The firm should test that with clients before promising anyone a career from it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 in 2036 I would still need a full wage, but a decade would let Daniel and me clear his mother's repair costs and grow our reserve. Robots around 2039 might affect his caretaker duties, while my desk work changes in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners next year for a paid monthly meeting service for six family-run shops, with the fees going to Quay Accounts and my salary unchanged while we test it. We'd save toward six months of expenses; in the first year after 2036, if the service covers my salaried hours, I'd stay, and if the firm cuts that paid work I'd apply for an advertised salaried college finance post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy, but I have time to test the service and build savings. The date is far enough away to plan, not far enough to ignore.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the meetings worth repeating?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask each owner to bring three months of invoices and show which payments are late. If four of six renew at a fee covering staff time, I'd tell the partners to continue; otherwise the service has not paid for itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your family plan change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel and I would consider a child only after the repair is paid, six months of bills are saved and our wages have been steady for a full year. I want family close, but I want the baby to have a secure home.

say: I would test **paid monthly meetings** with six family-run shops through Quay Accounts.
I would continue only if **four renewals** cover staff time.
think: My desk faces **2036 AGI**, while Daniel’s caretaker work faces later robot risk.
A decade might provide a **six-month cushion** and time to settle the repair bill.
do: Seek approval for **six shop meetings**; continue after 2036 only if four renewals cover staff time.
Build **six months of bills** after settling the family roof repair.
Apply for a **posted salaried college role** if paid firm work falls after 2036.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, but can test fees and savings before 2036.
S4.quote: I want family close, but I want the baby to have a secure home.
fieldNote: The meeting service is **salaried firm work** with fees going to Quay Accounts, not personal side income.
Her child plan needs the **repair paid**, six months saved and a full year of steady wages.

steps.text: Continue partner-approved shop meetings after 2036 if four of six renewals cover paid staff hours
Build six months of household bills after roof repair is paid
Apply for advertised salaried college finance post if paid firm work falls after 2036
Consider a child after repair is paid six months saved and one steady year

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my review salary could vanish before Daniel's mother's roof is fixed. A written staffing decision, paid time to practice payroll disputes and a posted salaried opening would help. I can make a budget; I cannot budget a job into existence.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how many junior accountants will be allowed to learn the hard work if software takes the easy returns. My own skill came from someone patient enough to correct me on a real file.

headlineQuote: I can make a budget; I cannot budget a job into existence.
portrait: Uma, **27**, leads a review desk at Quay Accounts and holds a master’s degree and chartered qualification.
Her **typical salary** and three-month cushion support a shared flat with Daniel, with some accounting jobs nearby.
She uses AI **occasionally after colleagues**, verifies tax sources and prefers paid trials before wider use.
A family **roof bill** shapes her saving, while 2028 AGI threatens her desk salary most.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end her review salary before Daniel’s mother’s roof is repaired.
whatWouldHelp: A **written staffing decision**, paid payroll practice and a posted salaried opening would let her plan.
